The last Loeb volume of Dio Cassius holds books seventy-one through eighty in Byzantine epitome, with the set's index. Earnest Cary's translation closes the eighty-book history that Dio wrote around 230 CE. The story runs from Hadrian to Severus Alexander, close to the author's own lifetime.

Marcus Aurelius fights on the Danube, Commodus struts and falls, and the Severan house takes the throne. Dio served under these last emperors, so his tale turns into near-witness report. The history that began with Aeneas ends in his own senate years. No other Roman narrative covers so long a span in one voice.
froude-history-england-vol-9:
The road to the Armada runs through the ninth volume of Froude's History, from 1856. The Babington plot aims at Elizabeth's life and Mary's release. Mary stands trial and dies at Fotheringhay, while Spain prepares its vast fleet for war.

Froude builds the tension chapter by chapter toward the coming storm. Readers feel the danger long before the sails appear in the Channel. Secret letters, Walsingham's spies, and Philip's slow armada drive the tale. The volume forms the penultimate act of his Tudor epic, a fuse burning toward the famous deliverance that his next book celebrates in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-9:
Thompson's minutes record the first plenary session of the Potsdam Conference, at 5 p.m. on July 17, 1945. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The three leaders met with Truman in the chair, a choice Stalin proposed and Churchill seconded.

Truman asked leave to propose agenda items, and Stalin agreed. Eden won the point that all members could add items of their own. Truman then read his proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers. His second paper, on Germany, he handed in for study without reading it. Churchill asked if the matters were not to be considered now, and Truman replied he was merely proposing agenda items. Churchill moved that the first item go to the foreign ministers. Stalin agreed, but questioned China's place in a council meant for European problems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-9:
Ginnie Mae meets its mission but faces a changing market, GAO concludes in report GAO-06-9, dated October 31, 2005. Ginnie Mae is a wholly owned government firm. It backs mortgage securities built from loans insured by federal housing programs.

Congress noted that Ginnie Mae's share of the mortgage security market had fallen sharply. GAO studied the state of that share and of guarantee volume. It weighed what a smaller share could mean. It also set out the hurdles Ginnie Mae faces and steps it has taken, or could take. The report gives housing finance readers a clear snapshot of a public backer under market pressure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-9:
The Darfur crisis and aid efforts fill GAO-07-9, a report dated November 9, 2006. Conflict broke out in Darfur, Sudan, in 2003. Rebels, government troops, and the Janjaweed militia drove about 2 million people from their homes. Over 1.9 million others need aid to survive. The United States has given help since October 2003. It also backs the African Union Mission in Sudan. GAO reviewed the aid flow and the peace mission's work.

The United States provided nearly $1 billion in aid from fiscal years 2004 through 2006. Food aid made up over 68 percent of that total. Malnutrition and death rates fell between 2004 and 2005. Attacks on aid convoys and banditry block deliveries, though. Sudan's government restricts access to displaced communities. The African Union force struggles with funding and logistics. GAO urged a lessons-learned review of the mission. The State Department backed that call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-9: This 2007 GAO report studies D.C.'s voucher plan, which lets poor kids use public money for private school. GAO found the program's books and daily running needed tighter rules and cleaner steps. The report lands in the middle of a hot school-choice fight — asking whether the program's promise to kids was matched by grown-up management.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-9:
Haunted houses of the mind fill the ninth volume of Archer's 1908 Ibsen. Rosmersholm traps its lovers in a manor where the past poisons every present hope. The Lady from the Sea gives us Ellida, torn between a safe husband and a mysterious sailor who claims her from the deep.

Guilt drives Rosmer and Rebecca toward the mill-race in a ending of quiet horror. Ellida's story moves the other way, toward freedom granted and freely chosen. These middle plays show Ibsen leaving social realism for symbol and mystery. Their strangeness rewards slow reading or a darkened stage. Few volumes in the set feel so unlike anything written before them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-abba-ha-l: Aaron Abba ha-Levi ben Johanan, a prominent rabbi, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was born about the close of the sixteenth century and died in Lemberg on June 18, 1643. He presided over a rabbinical college in Lemberg. His decisions appear in the responsa of Abraham Rapoport, Joel Sarkes, and Meir Lublin. Lublin spoke especially highly of him, the entry notes. In one case Aaron is shown condemning rigorism, or excess strictness, in the Law.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-9:
Part Nine calls New Orleans the metropolis of the South. Chapter 41 finds the city's approaches familiar and unchanged. High river water lifts boats level with the levee rim. Travelers look down into upper windows of houses below.

Old brick salt-warehouses cluster at the city's upper end. War news once turned their cheap salt into metaphorical gold overnight. The proprietor woke to find prices risen to dizzy heights. Vast plank wharves remained as Twain remembered them. Plank wharves stretched vast and unchanged along the landing. Aladdin's lamp, Twain jokes, had touched those vulgar salt sacks.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-9:
John Chrysostom, the golden-mouthed preacher of Antioch and Constantinople, enters Schaff's Nicene Fathers in volume nine of the first series, from 1886. The volume holds his treatise On the Priesthood, his ascetic writings, and select homilies and letters. The Homilies on the Statues close it.

On the Priesthood, a dialogue with his friend Basil, weighs the terrors of leading souls and Chrysostom's own flight from ordination. The Statues homilies were preached as Antioch trembled after a riot tore down the emperor's images, awaiting his revenge. Chrysostom calmed the city week by week. The volume shows why his preaching is still read for its force and pastoral nerve.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-9:
Hilary of Poitiers and John of Damascus, four centuries apart, share volume nine of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Hilary was the West's champion against Arianism, exiled for the faith he defended. John, a monk near Jerusalem under Muslim rule, was the last of the Greek fathers. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Hilary's work on the Trinity brought Greek theology into Latin dress. John's Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith then sums up the whole Greek tradition in one ordered system. His defense of holy images, written from beyond the empire's reach, helped win icons their place. The volume bridges the first councils and the age of Byzantium.
skilled-assistance-ship-s-company-part-9:
Skilled Assistance comes from Ship's Company by W. W. Jacobs, and a night-watchman at Wapping tells the tale. He grouses about a woman who keeps asking whether the Silvia has come up. She has, he says, called four or five times in a week, and she scolds him as if he were paid to wait on her alone.

Her temper puts him in mind of Cap'n Pinner, who sailed the schooner Snipe between Wapping and Hull. Pinner had a small cottage near Hull, and his wife's father, a man of near seventy, lived with them there. The watchman's pub talk sets up a yarn about help given, and help that may not be all it seems.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-9:
The burial of Jesus opens volume nine of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. Matthew's text tells how Joseph of Arimathea begged the body, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb, rolling a great stone to the door. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary kept watch across from the grave.

Next, an angel rolls back the stone at dawn and tells the women Christ is risen. Then comes the walk to Emmaus. Doré's dark tomb scenes give way to bright ones as the gallery nears its close.
the-head-of-the-family-sailor-s-knots-pa:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Head of the Family, a story in Sailors' Knots, dated 1909. Mr. Letts leaves his ship by joint agreement after working as cook on the schooner Curlew, a job he took after years on long voyages. The crew musters to see him off, and their harsh words from the quay at Dunchurch show how his cooking was judged.

Letts takes a room at a seamen's lodging-house and sits by the sea to plan what comes next. A middle-aged woman joins his bench, and he asks her, out of curiosity, how long she would boil a piece of beef. She tells him she lost a son at sea, and that he puts her in mind of the boy.
the-madness-of-mr-lister-captains-all-bo:
W. W. Jacobs's The Madness of Mr. Lister is the ninth book in his Captains All series of sea stories. Old Jem Lister of the Susannah is possessed of two devils, Jacobs says: the love of strong drink and avarice. The two meet in one habit, getting a drink without paying for it. When Lister pays, his avarice preaches him a teetotal lecture; when he reforms, his thirst sends him cadging at public-house doors, to his shipmates' shame.

His crew finally sends Bill Henshaw as spokesman, whose remarks leave little to be desired for violence and nothing unsaid for profanity. Their demand is simple: turn over a new leaf, and stand the men a round at the Goat and Compasses out of his hoarded sovereigns. Lister answers with a senile, venomous laugh and goes on deck to glower.
the-persecution-of-bob-pretty-odd-craft-:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Persecution of Bob Pretty as part of his Odd Craft tales. An old man on his bench outside the Cauliflower inn, beer at his elbow and a churchwarden pipe smoking, entertains two resting young men with talk of Claybury. Poaching, he says, is not what it used to be in these parts.

He points out Bob Pretty, the slyest, most artful man who ever lived in Claybury, who never did an honest day's work and never lacked the price of ale. Bob's worst time came after old Squire Brown died, when a rich Londoner named Rockett took the place and game preserving tightened. Jacobs's humor rests on the old man's voice.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-9:
Part 9 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XXXII, Coronation Day. The narrative steps backward a few hours to Westminster Abbey at four in the morning. Torch-lit galleries are already filling with people content to sit seven or eight hours for a sight they may not hope to see twice: the coronation of a king. London and Westminster have been astir since the warning guns boomed at three.

The packed galleries wait through the dragging hours. The great north transept stands empty for England's privileged ones. On the carpeted platform the throne rises on four steps. Inside its seat lies the stone of Scone, a rough flat rock on which generations of Scottish kings were crowned. Throne and footstool are covered with cloth of gold. At last daylight softens the torchlight, and at seven the first peeress enters in splendour.
the-substitute-deep-waters-part-9:
W. W. Jacobs tells this Deep Waters story through his night watchman. The man has just returned to the office fire from the wharf bell. It was the third that week from mischievous boys. The watchman complains: some people have boys, other people have the trouble of them. He launches into the worst boy he ever knew. The lad was a former office-boy there.

The lad was undersized. His face was the colour of bad pie-crust, his eyes like shoe-buttons. He stayed late pretending to work for a rise. One eye watched the ledger. The other eye watched the watchman. Once the boy found the watchman gone for half a pint. He raised a false alarm of drowning. A policeman, two carmen, and the crew of the Maid Marian turned out. The watchman never forgave the trick. Then a little steamer, the Eastern Monarch, enters the tale.
un-ga-res-9:
Peoples who could not yet rule themselves had no seat at the first General Assembly, and Resolution 9, passed on 9 February 1946, speaks for them. The text notes that whole peoples still lacked a full share of self-rule and had no voice in the hall. Chapters XI, XII, and XIII of the Charter treat their plight as a core concern for peace and the common good.

Under Chapter XI, states that rule such lands accept a sacred trust. The good of the people in those lands comes first. The ruling states must build self-rule and help free political life grow, step by step. Chapters XII and XIII add the trusteeship system, UN watch over lands placed under its care.
un-ga-res-a-69-9: Joint work with the League of Arab States fills Resolution A/69/9, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls past votes on the tie and the League's own pact, which charges its council with finding ways to work with world bodies for peace. It takes note of the Secretary-General's Agenda for Peace and its call for closer work with regional groups. A 2013 Security Council meeting on such joint work is welcomed.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 9 (I), adopted by the General Assembly on 9 February 1946, is the Assembly's first word on peoples who do not yet govern themselves. It states that the Charter's Chapter XI obligations toward Non-Self-Governing peoples were already in force and did not depend on any later agreement.

The Assembly welcomes the stated intention of states administering League of Nations mandates to negotiate trusteeship agreements. It notes one territory's move toward independence. It asks the Secretary-General to include in his annual report a summary of the political, economic, social, and educational information transmitted under Article 73e of the Charter. Coming months after the Charter took effect, the resolution put the Assembly on record that colonial obligations were immediate duties, not future promises.

Resolution 69/9 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, covers cooperation between the United Nations and the League of Arab States. It asks the two secretariats to deepen consultations and information exchange. The exchange spans political, economic, cultural, disarmament and peacebuilding work. It calls for the review of their 1989 cooperation agreement to be sped up. It schedules the twelfth sectoral meeting for Cairo in early 2015, on human rights. It schedules the thirteenth general meeting for 2016.
un-sc-res-9:
Access to the World Court for states outside its Statute was set by the Security Council on 15 October 1946. Article 35 of the Court's Statute lets the Council fix the conditions. A state that is not a party to the Statute may still come before the International Court of Justice. It must first deposit a declaration with the Court's Registrar.

By that declaration the state accepts the Court's jurisdiction under the Charter and the Statute and Rules of the Court. It promises to comply in good faith with the Court's decisions. It also accepts the duties of a United Nations member under Article 94 of the Charter. The declaration may cover one named dispute or disputes in general, present or future. A state may accept the Court's compulsory jurisdiction, though not against Statute parties without agreement. The Registrar keeps the originals and sends certified copies to all states concerned.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 9, adopted unanimously on 15 October 1946, opens the World Court's doors to countries outside its own statute. The International Court of Justice had just begun work, and some states were not parties to its statute. Under the UN Charter, the Council sets the conditions on which such states may appear before the court.

The resolution sets one main condition: the state must first deposit a declaration accepting the court's jurisdiction under the Charter, the statute, and the rules. It must promise to comply in good faith with the court's decisions and accept the duties members owe under Article 94 of the Charter. Declarations may cover one dispute or disputes generally, including compulsory jurisdiction.
